To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have generated an HIV-1 GAG subtype panel with a broad diversity and that several HIV-1 antigen detection tests exhibited problems, especially with non-B subtype detection.

we created a panel of 42 HIV-1 pVLPs that are useful to evaluate the detection limits and subtype detection of pVLP-detecting tests, that several tests had problems detecting pVLPs from non-B subtypes and that heat treatment lowered the detectability of HIV pVLPs in 2 of the 3 tests.

we generated an HIV p24 antigen panel with a broad diversity and used it to evaluate the performance of 4th generation HIV antigen/antibodies tests and antigen-only tests for their detection limits and breadth of subtype coverage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of p24 antigen detection methods with improved performance.
the generation of an inexhaustible p24 panel for standardised test evaluation.
the development of a standardised panel of HIV-1 GAG subtype VLPs for the evaluation of p24 detection by diagnostic tests.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current generation of 4th generation and antigen-only tests are still not sufficiently sensitive for routine use in early HIV-1 detection.
none of the tests are suitable for routine use in non-B subtype prevalent settings.

the current generation of 4th generation HIV tests are not suitable for early diagnosis of HIV infection in non-B subtypes and that further research into the development of a more sensitive p24 test is required.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 4th-generation HIV tests are not equally sensitive in the detection of p24 antigens of all HIV-1 sub-types.
the current generation of 4th generation and antigen-only tests have a high sensitivity, but their ability for subtype discrimination is variable.
the current generation of p24 tests has a broad detection range and is able to detect most of the circulating HIV-1 sub- and recombinant types.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current p24 detection assays are not sufficiently sensitive to detect all HIV-1 p27 variants, and that the current WHO p24 standard is not representative for the diversity of HIV-1.
the detection of HIV-1 primary infection is still not a standardised process.
the current generation of HIV p24 tests are not yet suitable for a universal application in HIV testing.
